# Converting with `pysacd convert`

`pysacd convert` turns an SACD image (or a PS3 disc) into tagged DSF, FLAC or WAV files with your own naming. For `sacd_extract`-compatible output use `pysacd-extract` instead.

```
make                                      # builds src/pysacd/_sacdconv.so
pysacd convert disc.iso                   # stereo area -> DSF, tagged
pysacd convert -f flac disc.iso           # 24-bit/88.2 kHz FLAC
pysacd convert -f flac -r 176400 -a both -o ~/Music disc.iso
pysacd convert -n disc.iso                # dry run: show the MB match and paths
```

Requirements:

- gcc and make
- `flac-devel`, for FLAC output only. `make` builds without it, and DSF and
  WAV still work.
- `mutagen`, for tagging.

The defaults are set in `~/.config/pysacd/config.toml`, using the same names
as the long options with underscores; command-line flags override them:

```toml
dir_template = "{albumartist}/{year} - {album} [{edition}]"
file_template = "{disc_prefix}{tracknumber:02d} {title}"
format = "flac"
```

Template fields:

- Album: `albumartist`, `album`, `date`, `year`, `originalyear`, `label`,
  `catalognumber`, `barcode`
- Track: `artist`, `title`, `composer`, `tracknumber`, `tracktotal`
- Disc: `discnumber`, `disctotal`, `disc` (`Disc N`, only set on multi-disc
  releases), `disc_prefix` (`N-`, multi-disc only). These come from `--disc N/M`
  if given, otherwise from the MusicBrainz match, otherwise from the TOC's
  album set fields (set size and sequence number).
- Area and format: `edition` (from `stereo_edition` or `multichannel_edition`),
  `layout` (`Stereo`, `5.0` or `5.1`), `channels`, `format`

**Different discs, same folder.** Before writing, `pysacd convert` checks
whether the target folder already holds tracks of a *different* disc. That
means a different MusicBrainz release, or failing that a different catalogue
number or barcode. Discs of one set (same album and artist, different disc
numbers) and re-runs of the same disc are fine. On a clash, the new disc goes
to `<folder> [<catalogue number>]` and a warning says so.

Some sets are mastered with every disc claiming to be disc 1 of 1, such as
Miles Davis's *Live-Evil*. For those, the warning may add a hint: when the
discs share title, artist and label and their catalogue numbers differ only
in a trailing counter, it suggests re-running with `--disc N/M`. pysacd never
acts on that guess by itself. With `--disc` the discs share one folder,
separated by `{disc_prefix}`.

Tracks that already exist are skipped unless `--overwrite` is given, and the
run summary says how many were skipped.

Tracks are cut at their timecodes, without the pauses between them. `--pauses` (config
`pauses = true`) includes them, with the same track ranges as `pysacd-extract -b`: each
pause goes with the track before it, and track 1 starts at the area start. Use it to match a
library extracted with pauses, so the DSD of each track is identical.

`pysacd convert` refuses to run as root unless `--allow-root` is given, because disc
images are untrusted input (see [security](security.md#running-as-root)).

Python format specs work (`{tracknumber:02d}`). Empty `[]` or `()` left by blank
fields are removed, and `/` inside values is replaced. `--portable-names` also
replaces characters that are invalid on Windows/SMB (always on, on Windows).

Names are NFC-normalised. Each folder or file name is cut to 240 bytes on a whole character
(a letter with its accents, an emoji sequence, a flag), never inside the extension. Two tracks
whose names differ only in case or Unicode form ("Intro" and "intro") would be one file on
macOS, SMB or NTFS, so the second gets " (2)". This applies to `pysacd-extract --templates`
too.

MusicBrainz data is checked field by field. A missing or wrongly typed value (a null title, a
list where a name belongs, a track number like "A1") is ignored, and the disc's own text is
used for it. Disc text in Shift-JIS, Big5, GB 2312 or KSC 5601 is decoded before anything
else looks at it, and an invalid byte sequence becomes "�".

How it works:

- **Audio:** one call into `_sacdconv.so` (through ctypes, which releases the
  GIL) produces every output for an area in one sequential pass over the image:
  - **Reader thread:** reads the frames the outputs need through
    [scarletbook-rs](https://github.com/aclater/scarletbook-rs) (#85), whose pool of decoding
    threads decodes DST ahead of it, and groups them into batches of 32 frames. Where a DSDIFF
    output keeps the DST frames as stored (edit master, `-p` without `-c`), scarletbook hands
    out each position's stored frame next to its decoded audio, from the same read.
  - **Worker pool** (`-j` or `--threads`, defaulting to the CPU count): converts DSD to PCM
    and lays out DSF blocks. scarletbook's decoding pool has one thread fewer, so the reader,
    which works on every frame, has a CPU of its own (#94).
  - **Writer thread:** writes every overlapping output in order. That covers
    DSF, DSDIFF (DSD or DST passthrough), WAV and FLAC.

  An ISO copy (`-I`) is written first, in one sequential pass, and the audio then read from
  that copy, so a PS3 is read only once. Even a single long DST track uses every core.
- **PCM (FLAC/WAV):** a three-stage linear-phase FIR (2.8224 MHz → 352.8 →
  176.4 → 88.2 kHz) with a stopband of about 105 dB and TPDF dither. The
  default gain is 0 dB, which puts SACD's 0 dB reference at −6 dBFS, so
  nothing clips; use `--gain-db 6` if you want louder files. Each batch is
  filtered with two frames of context on either side and trimmed by the exact
  filter delay. Track joins are therefore sample-exact (gapless), and the
  output doesn't depend on the thread count.
- **Tags:** the MusicBrainz release is found by barcode (the SACD's album
  catalog number) or by catalog number. The match is checked against track
  count, durations and ISRCs, and picks the medium for the right layer:
  MusicBrainz lists "Hybrid SACD (SACD layer, 2 channels)" and "…multichannel"
  as separate media. If there's no confident match, the disc's own text is used.
  Use `--mb-release ID` to force a release, and `--mb-text-search` to allow a
  fallback search by title and artist. FLAC gets Vorbis comments; DSF and WAV
  get ID3 tags (v2.3 by default). Both follow Picard's field names, including
  the MusicBrainz IDs.

## Submitting ISRCs to MusicBrainz

Most SACDs carry an ISRC for every track, and many MusicBrainz recordings are
missing theirs. pysacd can add them, which also helps later lookups (by
pysacd or anyone else) match the right release. Nothing is ever submitted
without asking.

```sh
pysacd mb-login --client-id ID              # once: OAuth sign-in, token saved owner-only
pysacd submit-isrcs -n album.iso            # dry run: show what would be added
pysacd submit-isrcs album.iso               # show the same table, ask, then submit
pysacd convert --submit-isrcs album.iso     # offer it after the MusicBrainz match while converting
```

- **Which release:** only one matched by barcode or catalog number, or named
  with `--mb-release`, never one found by title search. Track N of the area
  maps to track N of the matched medium (stereo and multichannel separately).
- **What's skipped:** malformed or all-zero ISRCs, the same ISRC on two
  tracks, ISRCs the recording already has, and ISRCs MusicBrainz already lists
  on a different recording. The table says why for each track.
- **Signing in:** register an application of type "installed" at
  <https://musicbrainz.org/account/applications> for the client id and
  secret, then run `pysacd mb-login`. The token lives in
  `~/.config/pysacd/musicbrainz-token.json`, readable only by you. Or pass
  `--mb-user NAME` to `submit-isrcs` for HTTP digest auth: the password is
  asked for each time (or read from `PYSACD_MB_PASSWORD`) and never stored.
- **Trying it out:** `--mb-server https://test.musicbrainz.org` (on both
  `mb-login` and `submit-isrcs`) uses the MusicBrainz test server, whose data
  is reset regularly.
- **Scripts:** `--yes` submits without asking. Without a terminal and
  without `--yes`, nothing is submitted.
